newsitem.title: SWEDEN: ATHLETICS-THREE KENYAN-BORN ATHLETES TO ATTEMPT WORLD MARKS.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-THREE KENYAN-BORN ATHLETES TO ATTEMPT WORLD MARKS.

text.p: Three Kenyan-born athletes will attack world records on Monday at the penultimate grand prix before the Athens world championships next month.
Stockholm Grand Prix organisers confirmed on Sunday that Moses Kiptanui, Daniel Komen and Wilson Kipketer would attempt world records at Monday's meeting.

Three times world champion Kiptanui, the only person to have broken eight minutes for the 3,000 metres steeplechase, will try to reduce further his mark of seven minutes 59.18 seconds set in Zurich two years ago.
Komen, who failed to qualify for the Atlanta Olympics last year, will attempt to capture Haile Gebrselassie's world 5,000 record of 12:44.39 set at the same Zurich meeting.
"I think I can do it" the confident Kenyan told reporters on Sunday.
And Kipketer, born in Kenya but now a Danish citizen, has set his sights on Sebastian Coe's 800 record of 1:41.73 run 16 years ago, the oldest track record on the books.
Kipketer, who was not allowed to compete in Atlanta, broke the world indoor record twice at the Paris world indoor championships last March.

There was another bonus for organisers when Morocco's Hicham el Guerrouj, who was only half a second outside Noureddine Morceli's world mile record in Oslo on Friday, confirmed he would run over 1,500 on Monday.
"He has had a standing invitation but he wanted to wait until after the Bislett Games," meeting director Rajne Soederberg said.
In the sprints, Maurice Greene, the new American 100 metres champion, takes on Trinidad's Ato Boldon, the Olympic silver medallist, over the 100 and 200.
Both men are coached by John Smith, who predicted last week that Donovan Bailey's world record of 9.84 seconds would soon be history.
"It's just a matter of time before the world record is going to be under 9.70, in the area of 9.68," Smith said.
"We want to take sprinting to a whole new level," he said. "We want to take it to where people don't think it can go. The world record is going to be a lot faster than it is now."
Local interest will focus on Ludmila Engquist, the Olympic 100 metres hurdles champion who formerly competed for the Soviet Union.
Engquist, who has been troubled by leg and back injuries, said she had recovered fitness.
"I think this will be my best race of the year," she said.

The meeting will mark the final international appearance of Sweden's veteran 400 metres hurdler Sven Nylander, who took part in the first world championships 14 years ago but has never won a medal in a global championships.
"It's my last race forever," Nylander said. " A world record tomorrow and I may reconsider my decision but that chance is slight."
